basis: The AHA record identifies an Indiana history doctorate in 1952, while the author of the other key's books earned a doctorate at Oxford and pursued an economics career. The different doctorates and careers support separate identities.

evidence.says: A contributor biography identifies Donna Dean as author of Warriors Without Weapons: The Victimization of Military Women.

basis: The author of the book is identified, but the sources found do not connect her to any of the H-Minerva reviews. The shared name and subject matter alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Geneviève Espagne reviewed René Sternke's Böttiger und der archäologische Diskurs in May 2010.
Geneviève Espagne's CV lists Aubin-Louis Millin et l'Allemagne (2005) and Schrift- und Schreibspiele (2002).

basis: The review and the books have a close subject connection, but the sources found do not explicitly link the reviewer to the editor or establish a shared institutional affiliation at the relevant time. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Relinde Meiwes wrote Arbeiterinnen des Herrn, published in 2000 and also a Bielefeld dissertation from 1998/99.
Relinde Meiwes, Berlin, reviewed Kosmos Diakonissenmutterhaus for H-Soz-Kult on 4 July 2005.

basis: The sources identify the book author and the reviewer, but do not establish that they are the same person. The shared name and related subject matter alone do not resolve the pair.

evidence.says: David Bitterling, Paris, reviewed Michèle Virol's Vauban for H-Soz-Kult on 18 June 2005.
David Bitterling is the author of L'Invention du pré carré, published in 2009.

basis: The sources identify each work but do not establish that the reviewer and the book's author are the same person. Their shared name and subject alone are insufficient to merge the keys.

evidence.says: Russell Poole reviewed Fallible Authors for H-Albion in January 2010; Margaret McGlynn of the University of Western Ontario commissioned the review.
The bibliography lists Russell Poole's Viking Poems on War and Peace, published in 1991.

basis: The review credits Russell Poole but gives no reviewer affiliation or other link to the author of Viking Poems. The commissioner's affiliation is not evidence of the reviewer's affiliation; the shared name and subject do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Jerry Thomas of the University of Wisconsin Oshkosh reviewed Erotic City in 2012.
Jerry Thomas joined UW Oshkosh as an assistant professor of political science in 2011–12 with a Ph.D. from the University of Kentucky.
Jerry Bruce Thomas, Shepherd history professor emeritus, earned a UNC Ph.D. and wrote the dissertation Coal Country.

basis: The reviewer's UW Oshkosh affiliation matches a newly appointed political scientist with a Kentucky doctorate. The Coal Country author had a UNC doctorate and a long career at Shepherd; these distinct doctoral and career records indicate different people.

evidence.says: Michael Coffey, editor at the N. C. Office of Archives and History, reviewed Basil Wilson Duke in 2006.
Michael W. Coffey received a history Ph.D. from Southern Mississippi and began work on North Carolina Troops in 2004.
Phaedra is edited by Michael Coffey, emeritus reader in Greek and Latin at University College London, and Roland Mayer.

basis: The reviewer's North Carolina archives career and the Phaedra editor's career in Greek and Latin at University College London indicate two different scholars. The identification of the reviewer with the North Carolina Troops editor is inferred from their shared name, institution, and overlapping years.

evidence.says: The publisher credits Firefight at Yechon to Charles M. Bussey and says he retired from military service in 1966.

basis: The publisher identifies the book's author, but the sources found do not connect him to the author of the 1975 thesis The Lost Opportunity of 1853. The shared name and compatible dates do not establish identity.

evidence.says: Margaret Moore is a Queen's political theory professor with an LSE PhD; her books include Foundations of Liberalism (1993) and A Political Theory of Territory (2015).
Margaret Moore, author of Foundations of Liberalism, earned a PhD at the London School of Economics in 1989.

basis: The 1943 thesis and the political theorist's later career suggest different people, but no source found establishes the thesis author's identity or an incompatible career. The available evidence does not establish a link or a definite separation.

evidence.says: Cites Richard H. Condon's 1964 article, ‘James Neild, Forgotten Reformer’.
Attributes The Moscow Parenthesis to Richard William Condon and identifies it as a 1969 University of Minnesota PhD thesis.

basis: The records contain distinct dissertations seven years apart, and the associated works identify their authors as Richard H. Condon and Richard William Condon. Together these support two scholars, although the difference is inferred rather than explicitly stated by a source.

evidence.says: Lists John L. Betts, The United States Navy and the Mexican War, University of Chicago, 1964.
Cites John Rickards Betts, Organized Sport in Industrial America, PhD dissertation, Columbia University, 1951.

basis: The two keys contain distinct doctoral dissertations, and sources associate the sport dissertation with John Rickards Betts at Columbia and a similarly titled naval work with John L. Betts at Chicago. The naval bibliography gives a different title preposition and year from the item, so the identification is inferred rather than certain.

evidence.says: The review credits One Woman's Political Journey to Lynn Musslewhite and Suzanne Jones Crawford.
Lynn R. Musslewhite and Suzanne Jones Crawford wrote an article on Kate Barnard; Musslewhite was a Cameron University history professor.
Cameron lists Lynn Ray Musslewhite in history and humanities with a Ph.D. from Texas Tech University.

basis: The Cameron record and coauthored article suggest a possible link, but the available admissible evidence does not independently connect the 1975 dissertation to that scholar or the book. The shared name and subject alone do not establish identity.
